Write P in the falling-factorial basis, P(x) = Σ b_j (x)_j with b_j integers. Divisibility by p^k for all integers x is equivalent to v_p(b_j) ≥ k − v_p(j!) for every j. The x^n coefficient is Σ_{j≥n} b_j s(j,n), where s(j,n) is the signed Stirling number of the first kind.

This coefficient can equal 1 exactly when some j ≥ n has p ∤ s(j,n) and k ≤ v_p(j!). Hence k(n,p) is the maximum of v_p(j!) over j ≥ n with p ∤ s(j,n).

To find which j qualify, reduce (x)_j mod p. For j = mp + r with 0 ≤ r < p, we have (x)_j ≡ (x^p − x)^m (x)_r (mod p). Every monomial of this product has degree at least m, and at least m+1 if r > 0. So a nonzero x^n coefficient requires m ≤ n, with m = n possible only when r = 0. For m = n and r = 0 the coefficient of x^n is 1. Therefore the largest valid j is pn, and

k(n,p) = v_p((pn)!) = n + v_p(n!).

**p = 11:** v_11(n!) = 1 for n = 11,…,15, so k = n + 1 = 12, 13, 14, 15, 16. The sum is 70.

**p = 13:** v_13(n!) = 0 for n = 11, 12 and 1 for n = 13, 14, 15, so k = 11, 12, 14, 15, 16. The sum is 68.

Total: 70 + 68 = 138.

ANSWER: 138
